title: Leaving Chicago, the trunk, and her son
summary: Jelly lacked money to ship the trunk; her son's college band and Jelly's letter to him.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: Did he take you to the station there?

Remember when he went away? Listen, he took me to the station and he couldn't find a man to carry my trunk down. Oh. That's what he told me, but that wasn't it. He didn't have the money to put my trunk because he was overweight. He told me I traveled like a country girl. I took everything I had and the trunk was so heavy that he couldn't handle it. But you know, I was home nearly three weeks before the trunk got there. Before he did? And it looked like to me, before the trunk came back to New Orleans, and it looked like to me it had just been sent a day or two, two or three days prior to the time it arrived here.
Yeah, but the thing of it is, I don't believe he had the money. Maybe not.
I don't believe. I've been broke too. There's no disgrace to be broke. No, indeed. But I don't believe he had the money. The station can be broke sometimes.

He didn't hear I have enough money to send me home. I wish I had my son's college picture here to show you with the band at school. Yeah. Because he always wanted to be like Uncle Jerry. Oh, really? He always, and my brother wrote him such a nice letter when he was in school. He was in school from, let's see, 35 until 39. He graduated in 39. And Jerry wrote him a nice letter, and he showed it to everybody. Yeah. He was so pleased to have him, Uncle. That was in the musical world.
